sentences.text: Pachycostasaurus dawni is the sole species within an extinct genus of marine reptile belonging to the family Pliosauridae.
The single known specimen measures approximately 3.1 meters in total length.
This animal is defined by its large, sausage-like ribs, gastralia, and shortened, thickened, double-headed cervical ribs.
Its barrel-shaped torso, short neck, and small flippers suggest it was not an agile swimmer.
The holotype possessed five pairs of stout, conical teeth located at the front of its lower jaw on the mandibular symphysis.
The head of Pachycostasaurus was about 20% of its total body length.
The specimen had at least 13 cervical vertebrae.
At approximately 3.1 meters long, this is the only known specimen of the species.
Its unique anatomy features large, sausage-like ribs and gastralia not seen in other plesiosaurs.
Five pairs of thick, conical teeth were found specifically at the front of the lower jaw.
The holotype fossil was discovered by amateur geologist Alan Dawn in a quarry in Peterborough.
The fossil was formally described in 1996 by Arthur Cruickshank, David Martill, and Leslie Noè.
Based on its anatomy, Pachycostasaurus was likely a benthic predator.
Its teeth suggest a diet of soft teuthoids like belemnites, bony fish, and possibly larger reptiles.
Pachycostasaurus likely played an important role in its food chain by transferring resources from the benthic to the surface food web.
Pachycostasaurus lived during the Middle Jurassic period, specifically between 165.3 and 161.5 million years ago during the Callovian stage.
Fossils of Pachycostasaurus have been found in the Oxford Clay formation of Peterborough, England.

It is debated whether Pachycostasaurus was allochthonous, having drifted into the marine basin from a freshwater or estuarine habitat, a possibility Cruickshank suggested might include coastal or deep-sea environments.
